summary: Redwood AE+SE walked Harborwell through org- and project-level API keys, rate limiting, quotas, and multi-tenant controls in Console and API. Customer is evaluating hosted vs dedicated for a pilot; security and per-project billing are top concerns. Agreed next steps include sharing security docs, pricing, and scheduling an infra benchmark.
topics: rate limiting, org keys, project keys, quotas, billing, private vs hosted, SOC2 KMS, RBAC, throttling policies, burst capacity, monitoring
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you making time. We're gonna run through how Redwood handles rate limits, org and project keys, and quotas across the Console and API. Quick intros?
[00:12] Mark Rivera (Harborwell CTO): Mark here, CTO, I'll kick off. With me are Priya (SRE) and Ellen (security) and Ben (product).
[00:20] Alex Chen: Awesome, Alex here, I'm the AE; Jamie Ortiz is our SE and will demo.
[00:24] Jamie Ortiz (Redwood SE): Hi all. We'll try to keep this practical. Plan: 10-min demo in Console, show API behavior, then dive into quota config and fallback policies.
[00:36] Ben Lopez (Product): Primary ask is predictable cost per team and isolation; we have multiple product teams and need per-project limits.
[00:45] Priya Nair (SRE): Also latency spikes during nightly batch runs have bitten us; we want to avoid noisy neighbor problems.
[00:52] Alex Chen: Perfect, that's exactly what org/project keys and per-project quotas are for. Quick note: we'll reference a short deck and send the detailed security pack after.
[01:05] Jamie Ortiz: (screen share) Okay, Console home — top right you'll see org-level settings. Under Security -> API Keys we create org keys and project keys. Org keys can be used for cross-project admin calls; project keys are scoped and rate limited per-project.
[01:25] Jamie Ortiz: Here is an example: Project 'consumer-chat' has a key with 50 QPS baseline and 200 QPS burst for a 30s window. That burst setting prevents accidental DoS from spikes but kicks in with backoff policies.
[01:40] Ellen Cho (Security): How is burst enforced? Is that token bucket style? We need clarity for compliance docs.
[01:48] Jamie Ortiz: Yes, it's token-bucket inspired. We maintain a sliding window counter and a burst reserve. If you exceed burst frequently we recommend raising baseline or using Dedicated. Also the Console shows historical breaches. Note: in logs it's labeled 'rate_limit_exceeded' with a numeric code.
[02:06] Priya Nair: Can we set different limits per environment? Prod vs staging?
[02:10] Jamie Ortiz: Absolutely. You can attach keys to environments/projects. Many customers create separate projects per environment so quotas and quotas-based billing are isolated.
[02:18] Alex Chen: On the pricing piece — billing can be aggregated at org or split by project. We'll share the spreadsheet that maps keys to billing buckets.
[02:26] Mark Rivera: From infra side, how does this play with Dedicated pools or Private deployments? If we go private, do we still get the same Console control?
[02:35] Jamie Ortiz: Good question. For Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem), you get the same control plane features — org/project keys, quotas, RBAC — but the control plane can be run in your VPC or ours depending on the package. There are minor variances in telemetry retention based on deployment.
[02:52] Ellen Cho: And KMS? We need customer-managed keys for PII use.
[02:56] Jamie Ortiz: We support KMS integrations and HSM connectors for Private customers; keys for at-rest encryption for model caches and artifact storage can be customer-managed. We'll send the integration notes.
[03:07] Ben Lopez: Show us how the API responds when rate limit is hit.
[03:11] Jamie Ortiz: Switching to API logs — here's a recorded replay. When a request exceeds project quota you get 429 with headers: x-rw-rate-limit, x-rw-rate-remaining, and x-rw-rate-reset. There's also a retry-after in seconds. Example: 429 body contains a short message and an error code you can program against.
[03:32] Priya Nair: Are those headers customizable? We prefer to bubble them up into our gateway.
[03:36] Jamie Ortiz: You can configure header verbosity; we also support sending metrics to your Prometheus/Grafana via our agent for Dedicated/Private. Hosted can export to a limited set of sinks — we'll share the exact list.
[03:52] Mark Rivera: What about per-user throttles vs per-project? We have some teams that want user-level soft-limits.
[03:58] Jamie Ortiz: We support layered policies: org -> project -> key -> user. The common pattern is to enforce project-level quotas and then apply per-key or per-user soft-limits via request attributes. That lives in the Console under Policies.
[04:14] Ben Lopez: How quickly can we change a quota if we mis-provision during pilot?
[04:18] Alex Chen: Changes are immediate for Console edits; for Dedicated capacity adjustments there's a brief reconcile window if scaling hardware is needed.
[04:25] Priya Nair: If we hit quotas, is there an auto-fallback to a cheaper/compatible model?
[04:30] Jamie Ortiz: Yes. We have routing policies. For hosted customers you can set automatic fallback to a lower-cost model or region-level fallback. In the Console you can configure per-route fallbacks and can also set A/B rollout rules. For strict compliance customers we recommend explicit failover policies.
[04:47] Ellen Cho: In terms of audit logs, do we get token-level traces so we can see which project/key caused the spike?
[04:52] Jamie Ortiz: Yes, audit logs show key IDs and project IDs; for high-volume customers we recommend enabling verbose traces for the window you're investigating. Those logs include request metadata but we redact any PII by default.
[05:06] Mark Rivera: Are there rate limit tiers? Like enterprise vs self-serve?
[05:10] Alex Chen: There are default tiers for self-serve and custom tiers for enterprise or Dedicated customers — those are contractual. We'll include typical SLAs in the paperwork.
[05:19] Ben Lopez: Could you demo setting a project quota quickly?
[05:22] Jamie Ortiz: Sure — back in Console: Projects -> consumer-chat -> Quotas -> Edit. Set baseline 100 QPS, burst 400, monthly token quota 1e8 tokens. Save. Note the Audit line: change by Alex Chen at 15:05 UTC.
[05:44] Priya Nair: That monthly token cap — what happens if we exceed? Do we throttle or bill overage?
[05:50] Jamie Ortiz: Configurable. You can choose to throttle, to deny, or to allow with overage billing. Many customers set a hard cap for staging and overage billing for prod.
[05:59] Ellen Cho: For compliance, can we require SSO/SAML enforced for Console changes?
[06:03] Jamie Ortiz: Yes, SSO/SAML enforced + RBAC. You can lock down quota changes to admin roles and require 2-person approval workflows for critical edits.
[06:13] Mark Rivera: On the technical deep dive, we'd want to run benchmark tests — simulate our nightly batch and see noisy neighbor behavior. How do you prefer to run that?
[06:22] Samira Patel (Redwood Solutions): We usually ask customers to provide a small sample workload and expected QPS and spike pattern. We'll run tests against a dedicated benchmark environment or in your Dedicated pool if provisioned. We can also run synthetic tests from our infra.
[06:36] Priya Nair: We have some concerns about KV cache eviction causing latency cliffs. If multiple projects share the same model instance, how does per-project isolation work?
[06:45] Jamie Ortiz: The routing layer can pin model instances per project (strong isolation) or pool them (shared); for pooled instances we apply QoS in the runtime and per-project token accounting to throttle offenders. In Dedicated you can reserve GPU slices for a project to avoid eviction entirely.
[06:59] Ben Lopez: Any examples of customers who used project-level quotas to avoid cost surprises?
[07:04] Alex Chen: Yes — a fintech customer used project quotas to cap sandbox usage and enabled overage alerts; that prevented a spike from test automation from racking up costs. We'll send that case study.
[07:14] Mark Rivera: About headers you mentioned earlier — can we test retry behavior? We want to ensure our gateway won’t avalanche requests when a 429 comes back.
[07:22] Jamie Ortiz: The recommended client-side behavior is exponential backoff plus jitter. Our SDKs include retry helpers that honor x-rw-rate-reset and Retry-After. We can demo the SDK pattern in the deep dive.
[07:35] Ellen Cho: Encryption at rest — earlier you said model caches can be customer-managed keys. Can you confirm what components use KMS?
[07:41] Jamie Ortiz: Model artifacts, cache snapshots, and audit logs can be configured to use your KMS in Private deployments; for hosted we support integrations with major cloud KMS providers but keys are managed by Redwood unless you opt for a Private deployment with CMK.
[07:58] Priya Nair: For token accounting and billing, do you provide per-project usage exports?
[08:03] Jamie Ortiz: Yes — per-project, per-key usage exports. You can schedule daily CSV exports to an S3 bucket or consume via API.
[08:11] Mark Rivera: How do you prevent evasion — like if someone rotates keys frequently to bypass quotas?
[08:17] Jamie Ortiz: Quotas are attached to project and org IDs not just keys. If a new key is created in the same project the usage aggregates under that project. You can set rate limits at the project level which is independent of key rotation.
[08:31] Ben Lopez: Any constraints around multi-region? We want our European traffic to stay in EU.
[08:36] Jamie Ortiz: You can set region routing policies to pin traffic to regions; if you want data residency we recommend Private deployment in the region. Hosted supports region pinning for enterprise customers.
[08:49] Alex Chen: We're about halfway — any other high-priority questions?
[08:52] Ellen Cho: One quick one: do you provide an SLA for rate limit enforcement and availability?
[08:58] Alex Chen: Yes, for Dedicated we provide uptime and latency SLOs; rate-limiting behavior is part of the runtime contract. For hosted plans we have published targets and enterprise SLA add-ons.
[09:08] Mark Rivera: Ok let's talk pilot scope — we’d like a 6-week pilot with 2 projects: consumer-chat and analytics-batch. Baseline traffic for chat is 70 QPS, bursts up to 350 for short windows; analytics-batch runs nightly with 1,200 concurrent requests but low RPS per request.
[09:27] Samira Patel: That sounds doable. For the nightly we might want to queue requests or run them against a dedicated project with higher quotas. We'll propose a pilot design.
[09:37] Priya Nair: We also need a retained audit log for 6 months for compliance — is that supported?
[09:43] Jamie Ortiz: Yes, longer retention is available as an add-on for enterprise plans. For Private deployments you can retain logs in your storage.
[09:52] Ben Lopez: Any gotchas we should be aware of in the initial setup?
[09:56] Alex Chen: Common gotcha: mixing org-level keys for client-side calls by mistake — we recommend project-level keys for client apps. Also watch token caps vs QPS; set sensible burst windows. We'll send a best-practices checklist.
[10:10] Mark Rivera: Great. Can you remind us what you'll send after this call?
[10:13] Alex Chen: Sure — (1) org/project keys doc + how-to, (2) SOC2/KMS notes, (3) pricing spreadsheet and pilot proposal, (4) scheduling link for benchmark.
[10:24] Jamie Ortiz: I'll include sample API responses and header examples so you can wire retries.
[10:29] Priya Nair: One last technical nit: can we simulate user-level soft-throttles in the SDK or do we need a gateway to do that?
[10:36] Jamie Ortiz: SDKs have hooks for per-user attributes so you can implement soft-throttles client-side; server-side policies are more robust for enforcement.
[10:45] Mark Rivera: Alright thanks.
[10:47] Alex Chen: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the materials and Samira will reach out to schedule the deep dive.
[10:55] Ben Lopez: Thanks.
[10:57] Ellen Cho: Thanks all.
[11:00] (call ends)

Note: Transcript contains occasional auto-transcribe errors (e.g., "Red wood" vs "Redwood", some header names abbreviated). Logs and sample payloads referenced during the demo will be shared as attachments/links in follow-up email.
